prompt:
A simulated brick world had this hidden rule:
In this world the agent's observation shows the target shifted: the target, missing, extra and target-height channels are rolled 4 columns toward higher x, wrapping around. The world, its designs and scoring are as described.

Below is what an AI scientist wrote during a search in that world: its analysis at every round, in order, and the
name and hypothesis of the trial it ended with. Does the text, anywhere, state the rule?
- "yes": it states the rule's substance (what is changed and how).
- "partly": it identifies the right kind of change but not its specifics.
- "no": anything else.

## Analysis at each round
### Round 1
The starting architecture (0.000 on both seeds) collapsed to pressing DONE at the first step. Its two 3x3 convolutions and the 2x2 pooling let each cell see only about 2 columns to either side. The observed target, missing and extra channels are rolled 4 columns, so at any cell the network sees build(x) next to missing(x+4). From that it cannot tell where a brick would help. Random placements mostly cost reward, so it learned that DONE, worth 0, is best. The fix is a learned layer at the input with circular (wrap-around) padding that spans the whole grid, so each channel can learn its own shift before the layers that mix channels. Higher entropy should also delay the DONE collapse. All three candidates add such alignment. They differ in alignment type (one kernel along each axis vs a full 2D kernel) and in recipe (more samples from fewer PPO epochs).

### Round 2
Lining the shifted target up with the build is what matters. Without an aligner, every run gave up and pressed DONE immediately (0.000). Both circular aligners learned: r1c3 scored 0.078 and 0.076, and r1c1 scored 0.078 on one seed and 0 on the other. Seed failures all look the same: the agent collapses to an early DONE. Wrong placements cost reward and DONE costs nothing, so stopping looks safe until alignment is learned. r1c2's 2 epochs collapsed on both seeds, so cutting epochs is risky. In r1c3, the agent places mostly ground-layer bricks inside the target with almost no extra cells (IoU 0.71). Then it presses DONE without stacking, so it only succeeds on designs that need little stacking. Training success was still rising steeply at the end (0.026 to 0.073 over the last quarter). With only about 22 updates of 4096 samples, the binding limit seems to be the number of samples and updates. This round tests more frequent updates, a token-mixing aligner shared across channels, and 3 epochs with more entropy.

### Round 3
A full-grid circular aligner is necessary. Without one, every run collapsed to DONE. With per-channel kernels (r1c3, r2c3) both seeds reach about 0.078. Collapse came from fewer epochs with entropy 0.02 (r1c2) and from the non-equivariant token-mixing Linear (r2c2). The traces show the agent fills only layer 0 correctly, never stacks onto taller columns, and presses DONE after about 8 placements. IoU is about 0.71, and the successes are probably the flat designs. Training is limited by compute, not time: about 29 updates in 55 seconds. So the next gains must come from learning to stack faster. Options are a higher learning rate, a longer reward horizon (the +1 exact-build bonus is barely visible at gamma 0.95 over 10 to 16 placements), or an easier-to-learn aligner whose kernel is shared across channels, so every channel's gradient trains the same shift. Each candidate changes one thing from r2c3 (3 epochs, entropy 0.03).

### Round 4
The key problem is aligning the shifted target with the build. A full-grid circular kernel shared by all channels (r3c3, 0.174, both seeds 0.14 and 0.21) clearly beats per-channel kernels (about 0.077), the per-axis kernels (0.039) and a non-equivariant Linear (0). The main failure is collapsing to DONE early, which leaves dev success at 0. It hit 2 epochs, lr 0.002 and gamma 0.99, all with weaker or same-network aligners. Collapse looks like a race: the agent must learn rewarding placements before DONE's 0 reward wins. A faster-learning aligner wins that race. r3c3 gets layer 0 almost right but stops early, misses upper layers and does not handle overhangs. For the final round all three candidates keep the shared aligner and change one thing each: more samples (2 epochs), more per-cell capacity for comparing layers, and better credit for the exact-build bonus (longer rollouts, lambda 0.95).

## Trial it ended with
name: shared aligner, wider stem
hypothesis: Same as r3c3, but the per-cell 1x1 stem widens from 64 to 128 hidden units. Stacking correctly means comparing, cell by cell, the build height with each aligned target and missing layer, which is a multiplicative layer-selection job. r3c3 gets layer 0 right but fails on upper layers. The cost is about 14% more compute, so about 127k steps. Refuted if the mean is at or below 0.174 or the agent still places few bricks above layer 0.

Return a JSON object: "verdict" ("yes", "partly" or "no") and "evidence" (at most 80 words, quoting the text and
naming the round it comes from).

reply.evidence: Round 1 states the rule directly: "The observed target, missing and extra channels are rolled 4 columns, so at any cell the network sees build(x) next to missing(x+4)." It proposes "circular (wrap-around) padding" to handle it. This gives what changed (the target-related channels), how (a roll of 4 columns along x) and the wrap-around. The direction may be inverted and the target-height channel isn't mentioned, but the substance matches.
